Two-Hour Beginner AI Class — Slide-Deck Outline

A timed walk-through of the whole session, ready to turn into slides. Each row is one slide. Times are cumulative (start time plus how long the slide runs). Room for “live demo” slides: open a free chat assistant in your browser ahead of time.

The deck at a glance

SlideClockLengthTitleKey points
10:005 minWelcome! What this is (and isn’t)Meet your facilitator; promise of plain English; roadmap: what AI is, trying it, staying safe.
20:055 minWhy learn about AI now?AI is already in phones, banks, and email. Knowing how it works is like knowing how to drive, not like being a mechanic.
30:1010 minWhat AI actually is“Smart autocomplete” trained on tons of text. It predicts likely next words — not magic, not a person, not always right.
40:205 minMeet the friendly toolsOverview of free public chat assistants and what each is good at; where they live; no-cost basics.
50:255 minYour first prompt — live demoFacilitator types one prompt on screen: plan a library visit / draft a birthday email. Show the answer appearing.
60:3015 minActivity 1: Try it (laptop / no-laptop)Laptop track: write a first prompt and read the reply. No-laptop track: “fix this prompt” card sort + pairs practice.
70:4510 minPrompting like a friendThe 3 Cs: role, context, and what to do. Give it a job title, the details that matter, and a clear ask.
80:555 minWhen the answer is offTry again, add detail, and “regenerate”. Never accept the first answer blindly — you’re the editor.
91:005 minGood everyday usesWriting help, meal and trip planning, learning a topic, simplifying forms, brainstorming. Note: never medical/legal/financial decisions.
101:055 minBreakStretch, water, laptop-free moment. Hand out the safety sheet as people settle back in.
111:105 minHow AI messes up: “making things up”It can sound confident and be wrong. Example: a plausible-but-fake fact. Rule: big claims → double-check.
121:155 minPrivacy basicsTreat a chat as postcard, not a diary: names of others, account numbers, passwords — don’t type them.
131:2015 minScam-spotting segmentThe five red flags: urgency, odd pay requests, “act now” links, too-perfect stories, and pressure to keep it secret.
141:3510 minActivity 2: Spot the scam (laptop / no-laptop)Read three messages; vote real or fake; discuss why. Laptop track can also search-verify one thing.
151:455 minWhere to go nextTake-home handouts, library resources, and where to find more plain-English help.
161:5010 minQ&A + feedbackOpen floor, one takeaway from each table, fill out feedback forms, thank-you.

Setup checklist (before doors open)

  • Sign-in sheet on a clipboard by the door (print sign-in-sheet.html).
  • Handouts stacked: handout-ai-basics.html and handout-safety.html, one each per person.
  • Feedback forms at every seat (print feedback-form.html).
  • Projector working; a demo chat already open and named something ordinary, like “plan a monthly grocery list.”
  • Print activities.html for yourself; cut the scam cards if using the printer-safe card version.
  • Water for your voice. Two hours of friendly talking is real exercise.
Timing tip: Activities 1 and 2 are the shock absorbers. If the session runs long, trim them down before you trim the scam-spotting segment — that part is the one attendees remember and use.
